# 6.8 The Stock Research Process: Key file (for the AI tutor only)

Do not reveal anything here before the learner has answered.

## Lesson facts relevant to the questions

- This is a brief lesson. The learner has studied market structure, barriers to entry and moats (Lesson 1.6, "Market Structure" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/1-6-market-structure/), financial statements and earnings quality (Lesson 3.7, "Financial Statement Analysis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-7-financial-statements/), financial ratios and ROIC (Lesson 3.8, "Financial Ratios" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-8-financial-ratios/), the DDM, DCF, WACC and relative valuation (Lesson 3.9, "Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-9-equity-valuation-ddm/–Lesson 3.11, "Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-11-relative-valuation/), the single-index model and idiosyncratic risk (Lesson 4.5, "The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-5-single-index-model/), market efficiency and behavioral biases (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/, Lesson 4.8, "Behavioral Finance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-8-behavioral-finance/) and active versus passive investing (Lesson 6.3, "Active vs. Passive Investing" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-3-active-vs-passive/). A calculator or code may be used to solve equations. Percentages in percentage points; variance in %².
- The lesson: EDGAR is free; the 10-K is audited, filed by large companies within 60 days of fiscal year end, with the business description, risk factors, MD&A, statements and notes worth reading; the 10-Q is unaudited; the 8-K comes within 4 business days of a major event; the proxy (DEF 14A) covers executive pay and the board; earnings calls often give guidance. The lesson does not compare the reliability of guidance and audited figures (left to Check C1).
- The lesson: Porter's (1979) five forces: rivalry, threat of entry, threat of substitutes, supplier power, buyer power; the weaker they are, the higher average industry profits. A moat (network effects, switching costs, scale, brands, patents) decides whether ROIC can stay above WACC. The lesson gives no formula linking growth, ROIC and value (left to Exercises Question 3).
- The lesson: a reverse DCF finds the growth implied by the price, then compares it with the company's history, the industry's size and similar companies' experience. Figure 3-1: price = a multiple of this year's free cash flow (horizontal axis 10–80), yearly growth $g$ for 10 years, then 3% forever; slider discount rate 7–11% (steps of 1, default 9); readout: at 9%, multiples 20, 40, 60 imply about 5.0%, 14.1%, 19.4%; at 7%, about −0.1%, 8.4%, 13.4%; at 11%, about 9.1%, 18.7%, 24.4%.
- The lesson: a thesis states why the price is below value, how one differs from consensus, possible catalysts, and evidence that would prove one wrong; write the case against seriously, with a pre-mortem (suppose a 50% loss in three years; the likeliest cause); counter confirmation bias and overconfidence; single stocks carry large idiosyncratic risk, so limit position size and keep individual stocks a small part outside the index core.

## Check question C1

The guidance for next year that management gives on the earnings call is audited, so it is more reliable than the historical figures in the 10-K.

Correct answer: False

Hint (give it after a wrong answer, without the verdict): What do auditors audit, results that have happened or forecasts? What motives might management have when giving guidance?

**Reference answer**

False. Audits cover financial statements of what has happened; guidance is management's forecast of the future, is not audited, and is covered by "forward-looking statement" disclaimers. Management may set guidance low so it can "beat expectations" later, or may be too optimistic. Guidance is useful, but should be checked against audited history and one's own analysis.

## Check question C2

US airline passenger numbers have grown over the long run, yet the industry's long-run average profit margin is very low, with several large airlines going bankrupt. By the five forces, the main reason is:

- (A) Several forces are strong: fierce rivalry with high fixed costs, price-sensitive passengers who compare fares easily, and strong bargaining power of suppliers such as aircraft makers, unions and airports ← Correct answer
- (B) Demand for air travel is too small
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): The question says passenger numbers have grown. Does large demand guarantee high profits? Who takes the profit?
- (C) Airline managers are generally less capable
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): If the whole industry has been like this for decades, is it more likely a matter of individual ability or of industry structure?

**Reference answer**

(A). Almost every force works against airlines: a seat is worthless once the plane leaves and fixed costs are high, so airlines cut fares to fill seats and rivalry is fierce; passengers compare fares online with nearly zero switching costs; aircraft come from two makers, and unions, airports and fuel prices squeeze profits too. The gains from growing demand go mainly to passengers and suppliers. The five forces show that industry structure matters more for profits than the size of demand.

## Check question C3

In Figure 3-1, raise the discount rate from 9% to 11%. For the same multiple (say 40), what happens to the implied growth, and why?

- (A) It rises, because future cash flows are discounted more, so higher growth is needed to support the same price ← Correct answer
- (B) It falls, because a higher discount rate means the market is more optimistic
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): With a higher discount rate, what are the same future cash flows worth today? For the value still to equal the price, what must growth do?
- (C) It stays the same, because the multiple has not changed
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Look at the curve and the readout: after changing the discount rate, does the growth at a multiple of 40 change?

**Reference answer**

(A). At a multiple of 40, implied growth rises from about 14.1% to about 18.7%. A higher discount rate lowers the present value of future cash flows, so for value to still equal the price, future cash flows must be larger, that is, growth faster. It also shows that a reverse DCF's conclusion depends on the discount rate used; judge the implied growth across a reasonable range of discount rates.

## Check question C4

A company has a wide moat, excellent management and steady growth, so its stock must be a good investment.

Correct answer: False

Hint (give it after a wrong answer, without the verdict): Does a stock's return depend on how the company performs, or on how it performs relative to the expectations built into the price paid? Do other investors know the company is good?

**Reference answer**

False. A good company is not necessarily a good investment; price is the key. The market usually knows which companies are good and reflects it in higher valuations (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/). If the price already implies high growth, the stock can return little even if the company keeps doing well, as long as it falls short of expectations. A thesis must explain how one's view differs from the expectations already in the price.

## Check question C5

Writing down before buying "what evidence would prove me wrong" mainly serves to:

- (A) Prevent explaining away bad news after buying, or holding on because one does not want to admit a loss ← Correct answer
- (B) Guarantee that the investment will not lose money
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Can writing down when one would be wrong change the stock price? Whose behavior does it change?
- (C) Make the thesis look more professional
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Think about how people often react after buying when the price falls and bad news appears (Lesson 4.8, "Behavioral Finance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-8-behavioral-finance/).

**Reference answer**

(A). After buying, people tend to seek information supporting their view (confirmation bias) and are reluctant to sell losers (the disposition effect, Lesson 4.8, "Behavioral Finance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-8-behavioral-finance/). Exit conditions written in advance are a standard set calmly, before any loss, that can be checked later, reducing after-the-fact rationalizing. They cannot prevent losses, but they can make losses smaller when one is wrong.

## Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)

A software company has free cash flow of 4 dollars per share this year, and its stock is at 200 dollars. Use a discount rate of 9.5%, with free cash flow growing 3% a year forever after 10 years.
(a) Use a reverse DCF to find the yearly growth in free cash flow over the next 10 years implied by the price (code or a calculator may be used to solve).
(b) An analyst says: "This company's free cash flow grew 20% a year over the past 5 years; it is a great company, and buying now is sure to make money." Evaluate this statement. Against what would you judge whether the implied growth is reasonable?

**Reference answer**

(a) The multiple is $\frac{200}{4} = 50$. Solve for $g$ in $\sum_{t=1}^{10} \left(\frac{1 + g}{1.095}\right)^t + \frac{(1 + g)^{10} \times 1.03}{(0.095 - 0.03) \times 1.095^{10}} = 50$, giving $g \approx 18.3\%$: free cash flow must grow about 18.3% a year for 10 years, reaching about 5.4 times today's level.
(b) The statement is wrong. The price already implies about 18.3% growth a year, not far from the past 5 years' 20%; whether investors make money depends on whether future growth beats this implied expectation, not on whether the company is great. Compare: historically few companies sustain more than 18% growth for 10 straight years, and growth usually slows as companies get bigger (reversion to the mean); whether the company's market is big enough for cash flows more than 5 times larger; whether competition and the moat can keep ROIC high; and how the implied growth changes at discount rates from, say, 8.5% to 10.5%. If these comparisons suggest 18% is already optimistic, "sure to make money" does not hold.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: multiple 50, implied growth about 18.3%, equation set up correctly.
- (b) OK: says returns depend on future growth relative to the implied expectation; gives at least two bases for comparison (similar companies' experience, market size, moat, sensitivity to the discount rate). Agreeing it is sure to make money needs revision.

Numeric answers: g = 18.3

**Common errors**

- Using a company's past high growth and its reputation as a "great company" as a reason to buy; not working out the growth already implied by the price or comparing it with how rarely companies sustain high growth.

## Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)

A company reports record annual profit. From its 10-K: revenue rose 10%, from 1 billion to 1.1 billion dollars; year-end receivables rose 40%, from 164.4 million to 230.2 million dollars; operating cash flow fell from the year before.
(a) Compute days sales outstanding for each year (year-end receivables / revenue × 365).
(b) The press release says "record results and strong growth". Evaluate this statement: what might these figures indicate? Which parts of the 10-K would you check further?

**Reference answer**

(a) Last year: $\frac{164.4}{1000} \times 365 \approx 60$ days; this year: $\frac{230.2}{1100} \times 365 \approx 76.4$ days.
(b) The statement deserves doubt. Receivables grew far faster than revenue, collection time lengthened by about 16 days, and operating cash flow fell: the profit growth did not turn into cash. Possible causes include looser credit terms or early revenue recognition to hit targets (such as stuffing channels at quarter end), customers less able to pay, or too small an allowance for bad debts (Lesson 3.7, "Financial Statement Analysis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-7-financial-statements/). Check further: MD&A's explanation of receivables and cash flow; the notes, for changes in revenue recognition policy, the bad-debt allowance and customer concentration; working capital changes in the cash flow statement; quarterly data (10-Q) to see whether revenue bunches at quarter ends; and the audit opinion and risk factors.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 60 and about 76.4 days.
- (b) OK: says profit did not turn into cash, gives at least two possible causes, and names at least two parts to check. Accepting "strong results" without these signals needs revision.

Numeric answers: dso1 = 60, dso2 = 76.4

**Common errors**

- Seeing record profits and concluding results are good; ignoring warning signs of earnings quality such as receivables growing far faster than sales, or operating cash flow lagging profits.

## Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)

A company's after-tax operating profit next year is 100 (million dollars), its cost of capital is 9%, and it plans to grow profit 4% a year forever. To grow, it must reinvest a share $\frac{g}{\text{ROIC}}$ of profit each year, and the rest is free cash flow, so its value is $V = \frac{E\,(1 - g/\text{ROIC})}{r - g}$.
(a) With an ROIC on new investment of 9%, 20% and 6%, what is the company worth in each case? How does each compare with no growth ($g = 0$, worth $\frac{100}{0.09}$)?
(b) A new CEO announces: "We will raise growth from 0 to 4%, greatly increasing shareholder value." Evaluate this statement. What would you need to know about the company to judge it? How does this relate to moats?

**Reference answer**

(a) With no growth, value is $\frac{100}{0.09} \approx 1111.1$. ROIC 9%: $\frac{100 \times (1 - 4/9)}{0.05} \approx 1111.1$, the same as no growth; ROIC 20%: $\frac{100 \times 0.8}{0.05} = 1600$, above no growth; ROIC 6%: $\frac{100 \times (1 - 2/3)}{0.05} \approx 666.7$, below no growth.
(b) The statement is not necessarily right. Growth creates value only when new investment earns an ROIC above the cost of capital; at an ROIC equal to the cost of capital growth leaves value unchanged; below it, growth destroys value, because reinvested money earns less than investors could get elsewhere. So one needs to know: what ROIC the new projects can earn, whether the existing business's ROIC stays above WACC, and whether growth extends existing advantages or enters areas with no advantage (such as expensive acquisitions). Keeping ROIC above the cost of capital for a long time is exactly the economic meaning of a moat (Lesson 1.6, "Market Structure" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/1-6-market-structure/); without one, competition pushes the ROIC on new investment toward the cost of capital, and growth no longer creates value. If management is paid on revenue or size growth, it may also be encouraged to pursue growth that creates no value (Lesson 1.9, "Information Economics" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/1-9-information-economics/).

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 1111.1, 1600 and 666.7, compared with 1111.1 for no growth.
- (b) OK: says growth creates value only when ROIC exceeds the cost of capital, that the ROIC of new investment must be known, and links this to moats. Agreeing that growth always adds value needs revision.

Numeric answers: v9 = 1111.1, v20 = 1600, v6 = 666.7

**Common errors**

- Thinking growth always creates value; ignoring that growth adds value only when the return on invested capital exceeds the cost of capital, and otherwise destroys value.

## Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)

An investor used to hold 100% in a stock index fund (volatility 16%). After months of researching a company, he decides to move 30% of the portfolio into its stock. The stock's volatility is 40%, and its correlation with the index is 0.5.
(a) Roughly what is the portfolio's volatility after the change?
(b) He says: "I've researched this company thoroughly, so this investment is much less risky than buying a stock I don't understand." Evaluate this statement and give advice.

**Reference answer**

(a) Variance $0.7^2 \times 16^2 + 0.3^2 \times 40^2 + 2 \times 0.7 \times 0.3 \times 0.5 \times 16 \times 40 = 125.44 + 144 + 134.4 = 403.84$ (%²), volatility about 20.1%, about a quarter higher than the original 16%.
(b) The statement is wrong. Research can raise the chance of being right (if he really has an information advantage), but it cannot reduce the stock's swings: idiosyncratic risks such as product failures, management changes, lawsuits and industry shocks (Lesson 4.5, "The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-5-single-index-model/) do not vanish because he understands the company. Overconfidence (Lesson 4.8, "Behavioral Finance" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-8-behavioral-finance/) makes people overrate the accuracy of their judgments, and other investors are researching the same company (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/). Advice: limit any single stock to a ceiling set in advance (say 5%), write down the thesis and the conditions that would prove him wrong, and set dates to review it; even if he is confident, use the method of (a) to see how much this position adds to the risk of the whole portfolio.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 20.1%, including the covariance term.
- (b) OK: says research cannot remove idiosyncratic risk, mentions overconfidence or competition among investors, and advises limiting the position. Agreeing that the risk is much lower needs revision.

Numeric answers: sd = 20.1

**Common errors**

- Thinking deep research lowers a single stock's risk, so a large concentrated position is fine; ignoring that research does not remove idiosyncratic risk, and the judgment may be wrong.
